PAPER: JHSMR Original Article Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Anion Gap is a Predictor of Elevated Serum Lactate in Patients Diagnosed with Sepsis without Shock in the Emergency Department Chollathip Bunyaphongphan, M.D., Theerapon Tangsuwanaruk, M.D., Borwon Wittayachamnankul, M.D., Ph.D., Chanon Changratanakorn, M.D. Department of Emergency Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Chiang Mai University, Chiang Mai 50200, Thailand. Received 3 December 2024 l Revised 30 January 2025 l Accepted 5 February 2025 l Published online 23 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: To determine whether high anion gap levels predict increased serum lactate >2 mmol/L, and to determine the best AG cut-off point for predicting serum lactate levels greater than 2 mmol/L and greater than 4 mmol/L. Material and Methods: This is a retrospective study among patients with sepsis without shock admitted to the emergency department of a tertiary care, university hospital. Anion gap and serum lactate were collected. Patients’ baseline characteristics and laboratory results were also incorporated to calculate the Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. Analysis of diagnostic accuracy and Receiver Operator Characteristics (ROC) was used to demonstrate the appropriate cut-off point of the anion gap for predicting serum lactate >2 mmol/L. Results: The study included 236 patients. Anion gap >12 mmol/L had a sensitivity of 93.3% (95%CI 88.2-96.6%) and a specificity of 13.7% (95%CI 6.8-23.8%) for predicting serum lactate >2 mmol/L. There was poor discriminative performance of the anion gap to predict serum lactate >2 mmol/L (area under ROC is 0.65; 95%CI 0.58-0.72). In contrast, there was good discriminative performance of the anion gap to predict serum lactate >4 mmol/L (area under ROC 0.83; 95%CI 0.77-0.88). The optimal cut-off point was anion gap > 18 mmol/L, which was good for predicting serum lactate >4 mmol/L. Conclusion: An anion gap >12 mmol/L is not suitable for assessing lactate >2 mmol/L; however, an anion gap >18 mmol/L can predict serum lactate >4 mmol/L in patients with sepsis who had mean arterial pressure (MAP) >65 mmHg. JSON: Name: anion_gap_lactate_predictor Title: Diagnostic accuracy and predictive modeling of anion gap for identification of elevated serum lactate in adult emergency department patients with sepsis and preserved mean arterial pressure Short Hypothesis: In adult emergency department patients with sepsis and MAP ≥65 mmHg, an anion gap >18 mmol/L predicts serum lactate >4 mmol/L with sensitivity ≥80% and specificity ≥70%. Related Work: Prior work has evaluated the anion gap (AG) as a surrogate marker for hyperlactatemia and outcome risk in infectious critical illness. Studies in ICU cohorts identified lactic acidosis as a common cause of wide AG but focused on patients with shock. Retrospective ED and mixed-cohort analyses reported weak correlation between AG and modest lactate elevations (e.g., >2 mmol/L) and poor specificity for mortality prediction when using low AG thresholds (e.g., >12 mmol/L). Other reports found stronger discrimination of AG for markedly elevated lactate (>4 mmol/L) and identified AG thresholds near 18–20 mmol/L as more predictive. Methodological limitations across studies include single-center samples, inclusion of heterogeneous shock states, inconsistent correction for confounders (e.g., hypoalbuminemia, renal failure, toxic ingestions), small sample sizes, and lack of prospective or external validation. Abstract: Many emergency departments lack rapid serum lactate testing, which impairs early identification of sepsis patients with clinically significant hyperlactatemia. We propose a structured diagnostic pipeline to evaluate whether the serum anion gap (AG), a routinely available laboratory value, can reliably predict elevated lactate in adult sepsis patients who are not hypotensive (MAP ≥65 mmHg). The pipeline comprises retrospective model development using ED electronic health records to compare raw and albumin-corrected AG against measured lactate, selection of optimal AG thresholds via receiver operating characteristic analysis, and external and prospective validation across multiple hospital sites. The primary contribution is a validated, parsimonious decision rule and predictive model that quantifies diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, AUROC) of AG thresholds for lactate >4 mmol/L and >2 mmol/L and assesses subgroup performance by comorbidity. Expected outcomes are calibrated diagnostic performance estimates, identification of limits of AG utility, and an evidence-informed triage rule that can guide lactate testing or referrals in resource-limited ED settings. Experiments: Datasets: Primary retrospective ED cohort of adult patients (age>15) meeting Sepsis-3 criteria with MAP ≥65 mmHg from a tertiary hospital EMR (dates: June 2019–Sept 2020; initial n=236); expanded retrospective cohort by extending dates and including two additional hospitals to achieve n≥1000; external validation set from 3 community hospitals (n≥500); prospective validation cohort over 6 months (n≥300). Inclusion: Sepsis-3 (ΔSOFA≥2), initial Na+, Cl-, HCO3-, serum lactate measured within 1 hour, MAP≥65 mmHg. Exclusion: transfers, incomplete labs, known toxic ingestion or diabetic ketoacidosis at presentation. Baselines: AG>12 threshold, AG>18 threshold, uncorrected bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L), base excess, qSOFA ≥2, SOFA score, and point-of-care lactate (gold standard). Models: (1) single-threshold diagnostic rule (AG raw and albumin-corrected), (2) logistic regression with AG and covariates (age, CKD, diabetes, infection source), (3) decision tree, (4) random forest. Evaluation metrics: AUROC with DeLong CIs, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV at prespecified thresholds, calibration (Brier score, calibration plot), Hosmer-Lemeshow, decision curve analysis, net reclassification improvement. Experimental setup: stratified 70/30 train/test split on each retrospective dataset; 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning on training set; threshold selection by Youden index and prespecified clinical thresholds; 2000-bootstrap for 95% CIs; DeLong tests to compare AUROCs. Ablation studies: (A) models with vs without albumin-correction of AG, (B) models excluding patients with CKD, (C) models without AG (covariates only), (D) comparison of raw AG vs estimated AG (if arterial blood gas absent). Subgroup analyses: CKD vs non-CKD, diabetes, age≥65, infection source (respiratory vs urinary). Statistical significance: two-sided alpha=0.05. Risk Factors and Limitations: Confounding causes of wide anion gap (diabetic ketoacidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols, ethanol, salicylates) may produce false positives; incomplete or missing albumin data will bias uncorrected AG estimates; single-center derivation risks overfitting and limited external generalizability; retrospective chart data may contain measurement timing mismatches (labs not simultaneous) and selection bias toward tested patients; low prevalence of lactate >4 mmol/L in some settings will reduce PPV and affect clinical utility; estimated PaO2 from SpO2 for SOFA components introduces measurement error; subgroup heterogeneity (CKD, chronic metabolic acidosis) alters AG-lactate relationship and reduces transferability; threshold optimization on retrospective data may not replicate prospectively (threshold overfitting); limited ability to detect rare alternative causes of AG elevation due to sample size; resource constraints at community sites may limit external validation completeness.
